name: Read and report imaging exams
summary: Radiologists with hospital privileges read the corporation's roughly 24,000 imaging studies a month and turn each into a signed report that goes to the emergency physician, ward team, clinic or community doctor who ordered it. They pick studies from a shared worklist by priority, compare with prior images, dictate into voice recognition, edit and sign, and phone critical findings directly. Emergency CT is read within an hour or two, even at night by the on-call radiologist from home, but overnight emergency X-rays wait for the morning list and outpatient studies queue behind emergency and inpatient work for a day or more. Delays and errors come from that queue, from tracking down physicians to report critical results, failed faxes and voice recognition mistakes left in signed reports.

baseline.org_archetype: A three-site Ontario community hospital corporation whose imaging is read by a fee-for-service radiology group of about 30 radiologists holding privileges at all three sites, using a shared RIS, PACS and voice recognition.
baseline.notes: Radiologists bill OHIP for the professional component; the hospital funds technologists and equipment. Reading times and queue waits are the author's estimates; the emergency turnaround benchmark comes from an Ontario academic hospital study.

trigger: A completed imaging study arrives on the radiologists' reading worklist.
end_state: A signed report is in the hospital record and delivered to the ordering physician, with critical findings phoned and documented; or an addendum has been issued and resent.

volume.seasonality: Follows exam volumes: lower outpatient work in summer and late December, a dip in 2020/21 when non-urgent imaging paused in the first COVID-19 wave, and winter peaks in emergency studies.

evidence.note: One report per exam; 298,482 exams in 2021/22 (hh2122), about 24,900 a month.

surge.cause: Winter respiratory season and emergency department surges add emergency CT and X-ray studies

evidence.note: Author's estimate, the same as dx-imaging-exam.

30 radiologists in the organisation file. About 24 FTE of reading at 130 productive hours a month is implied by the simulated reading time; radiologists also do fluoroscopy, biopsies, ultrasound checks and protocolling (counted in dx-imaging-exam and dx-imaging-booking).

roles.title: Diagnostic imaging booking and reception clerk

evidence.note: Outside priors, physician tracking and failed deliveries; not listed for this process in the organisation file.

systems.name: Radiology information system, PACS and voice recognition dictation
Hospital information system (electronic patient record with ADT, order entry, results, eMAR and clinical documentation)
Ontario Laboratories Information System and ConnectingOntario viewer

steps.name: Study lands on the reading worklist
steps.description: When the technologist completes the exam, PACS and the radiology information system place the study on the radiologists' shared reading worklist, sorted by priority (stat and emergency, inpatient, outpatient), modality and site, with the requisition scanned in.

next.condition: emergency study during in-house radiologist hours
emergency CT or ultrasound after hours

evidence.note: Priority mix is the author's estimate from the exam volumes: emergency 31% of exams (about 40% in-house hours, 20% after-hours CT and ultrasound read by the on-call radiologist, 40% after-hours X-rays read next morning), inpatient 17%, outpatient 52%.

steps.name: Open an emergency study during the working day
steps.description: The radiologist on the emergency or general reading list watches the stat flags on the worklist and opens emergency studies ahead of inpatient and outpatient work, usually within minutes for CT and within the hour for plain films.

evidence.note: lamb2015 reports median final emergency CT and ultrasound report times of 2.75-5 hours at an academic Ontario hospital; a community hospital's daytime emergency queue is estimated at 5-90 minutes before opening.

steps.name: On-call radiologist reads an after-hours emergency study from home
steps.description: The emergency physician or technologist pages the on-call radiologist, who logs into PACS from a home workstation, opens the CT or ultrasound and prepares to read it while the patient is still in the emergency department.

evidence.note: Author's estimate; the organisation file describes after-hours emergency studies read on call or by remote reading.

steps.name: After-hours emergency X-ray waits for the morning list
steps.description: Plain films taken in the emergency department overnight or on the weekend are interpreted by the emergency physician at the time and stay on the worklist until the radiologist arrives in the morning, when they are read first.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of overnight and weekend gaps in community-hospital plain film reporting.

steps.name: Open an inpatient study
steps.description: The radiologist works through inpatient studies between emergency cases, usually the same day, choosing first those flagged urgent or needed for a discharge decision.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Open an outpatient study
steps.description: Outpatient studies wait on the list until emergency and inpatient work is done; the radiologist reads them in batches by modality, so studies done late Friday are often read on Monday.

evidence.note: Author's estimate; the organisation file notes outpatient turnaround can stretch to days.

steps.name: Review the requisition, history and prior imaging
steps.description: The radiologist reads the clinical question on the requisition, opens prior exams and reports in PACS for comparison, and checks relevant lab results or notes in the hospital record or the provincial viewer.

next.condition: CT, MRI, ultrasound or nuclear medicine

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Request outside prior images
steps.description: The imaging clerk asks another hospital or clinic to push prior images to PACS or upload them to the regional image repository, then tells the radiologist when they arrive.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Interpret and dictate a plain film or mammogram
steps.description: The radiologist reviews the views, compares with priors, and dictates findings and an impression into voice recognition, using a template for normal studies.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of reading time per plain film.

steps.name: Interpret and dictate a CT, MRI, ultrasound or nuclear study
steps.description: The radiologist scrolls through the series, uses reformats and measurements, compares with prior exams and the sonographer's worksheet, and dictates a structured report with findings and an impression.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of reading time per cross-sectional study.

steps.name: Transcriptionist corrects the dictation
steps.description: For radiologists who do not self-edit, the voice file and draft text go to a medical transcriptionist, who listens to the dictation, corrects the recognition errors and returns the draft to the radiologist's signing queue.

error.defect_description: Mishears a word that changes meaning.

evidence.note: Author's estimate; voice recognition with self-editing was the norm by 2019, so only a small share goes to transcription.

steps.name: Edit and sign the report
steps.description: The radiologist reads the recognised text, fixes misrecognised words, laterality and measurements, and signs the report electronically, which makes it final and releases it.

error.defect_description: Voice recognition error left in the signed report.

control.basis: Only a radiologist with hospital privileges may sign a diagnostic imaging report (Public Hospitals Act medical staff rules)

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Phone the critical finding to the ordering physician
steps.description: The radiologist pages or phones the ordering or covering physician, reads out the finding, confirms it was understood and records who was told and when in the report.

control.basis: Hospital critical results communication policy (Accreditation Canada standard on timely communication of critical test results)

evidence.note: Author's estimate of share of reports with critical or significant unexpected findings.

steps.name: Track down the ordering or covering physician
steps.description: The imaging clerk looks up the referring office's number, the physician's answering service or the on-call schedule for the clinic or group, and calls until someone who can act on the result is on the line for the radiologist.

evidence.note: Author's estimate; after hours and for community physicians this can take hours.

steps.name: Release and distribute the signed report
steps.description: The radiology system sends the signed report to the hospital record and the emergency tracking board, faxes or sends it electronically to the ordering physician's office and copies listed on the requisition, and files it to the provincial imaging record.

error.defect_description: Fax fails or the referring physician is not in the directory.

next.condition: next-morning read differs from the emergency physician's interpretation

evidence.note: Author's estimate. Distribution through OntarioMD's Health Report Manager to physician EMRs is the author's general knowledge of Ontario practice; the system is not in the organisation file.

steps.name: Fix a failed report delivery
steps.description: The clerk works the failed-fax and unmatched-physician queue, finds the right fax number or adds the physician to the directory, resends the report and notes the delivery in the radiology system.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Tell the emergency department about a discrepant overnight read
steps.description: When the morning report of an overnight emergency X-ray differs from what the emergency physician saw, for example a missed fracture, the radiologist phones the emergency department so the patient can be called back.

control.basis: Hospital emergency discrepancy and patient callback policy

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Peer review a sampled report
steps.description: A second radiologist opens a randomly sampled study, reads the images blind or against the report, scores agreement on a standard scale and refers significant discrepancies to the department chief and the original reader.

control.basis: Diagnostic imaging quality program and peer review expected by Accreditation Canada and recommended by the Canadian Association of Radiologists

evidence.note: oag2018: peer review was not mandatory in Ontario in 2018 and three of the four audited hospitals had a regular program; sample share and discrepancy rate are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Issue an addendum to the signed report
steps.description: The original radiologist reopens the study, dictates an addendum that corrects or adds to the report, signs it, and phones the ordering physician when the change affects care; the system resends the amended report.

control.basis: Only the radiologist may amend a signed report

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

exceptions.name: Critical finding
exceptions.description: The radiologist phones an unexpected or critical finding; in 30% of attempts the physician cannot be reached and the clerk tracks down a covering doctor.

exceptions.name: Overnight emergency X-ray discrepancy
exceptions.description: The morning read finds something the emergency physician missed overnight and the patient is called back.

exceptions.name: Failed delivery
exceptions.description: The fax fails or the referring physician is unknown, so the report sits undelivered until the clerk resends it.

exceptions.name: Addendum
exceptions.description: A referring physician's query or a peer review discrepancy leads to an amended report.

exceptions.name: Outside priors
exceptions.description: Comparison images from another hospital are requested before the study can be read.

benchmarks.unit: calendar days from study on worklist to signed report
benchmarks.population: All studies in an Ontario community hospital, 2019-2022

evidence.note: Author's estimate weighting emergency (hours), inpatient (same day) and outpatient (one to five days, longer over weekends) studies; no published Ontario community-hospital turnaround figure was found.

benchmarks.unit: median hours, emergency abdominal and pelvic CT and ultrasound

evidence.note: Academic hospital with residents; a community hospital without an in-house emergency radiologist would be at or above the earlier figure after hours.

pain_points.description: Outpatient studies queue behind emergency and inpatient work and over weekends, so community physicians wait days for reports.

evidence.note: Author's estimate; the organisation file notes outpatient turnaround can stretch to days.

pain_points.description: Overnight emergency X-rays are not read until morning, so discrepancies with the emergency physician's reading lead to patient callbacks.

evidence.note: Author's general knowledge of community-hospital reporting coverage.

pain_points.description: Reaching a community physician to report a critical finding, especially after hours, takes repeated calls by the radiologist and a clerk.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

pain_points.description: Peer review of reports was voluntary and uneven, so reading errors were found by chance rather than by a routine check.

evidence.note: oag2018: no mandatory province-wide peer review; a 2013 review of one radiologist's work at a Toronto-area hospital prompted calls for one.

sources.title: 2021-2022 Annual Community Report (Halton Healthcare by the numbers)
sources.supports: 2021/22: 298,482 diagnostic imaging exams, 161,049 emergency visits, 45,256 surgeries, 4,690 births, 37,964 dialysis visits, 19,600 oncology visits, 62,508 mental health and addictions ambulatory visits, 40,428 fracture clinic visits, 3,220,658 laboratory tests, 5,228 staff, 931 physicians, dentists and midwives

sources.title: Impact of an in-house emergency radiologist on report turnaround time
sources.publisher: Canadian Journal of Emergency Medicine 17(1):21-26 (Lamb L, Kashani P, Ryan J, Hebert G, Sheikh A, Thornhill R, Fasih N)
sources.supports: The Ottawa Hospital emergency department, 1,624 abdominal and pelvic CT and ultrasound reports: median final report turnaround 5.00 hours in 2008, 3.08 hours in 2009 and 2.75 hours in 2010 after an in-house emergency radiologist was added; median preliminary (resident) report 2.40, 2.08 and 2.05 hours

sources.title: 2018 Annual Report, Volume 1, Chapter 3, Section 3.08: MRI and CT Scanning Services
sources.publisher: Office of the Auditor General of Ontario
sources.supports: Ministry priority levels for MRI and CT: emergency (P1, within 24 hours), urgent (P2, within 2 days), semi-urgent (P3, within 10 days), non-urgent (P4, within 28 days), targets set at the 90th percentile; before booking, radiologists assess the requisition, determine the type of scan and assign a priority, then a scheduler books a predefined slot; an MRI scan with contrast takes on average 40 minutes and needs at least two technologists on site, other MRI scans about 20 minutes with one; emergency scans were more than 30% of CT scans in 2017/18; MRI no-show rates 0.1% to 13.4% and CT 0.6% to 13% of scheduled appointments in 2017/18 (48,320 missed MRI and 57,916 missed CT appointments); 25-36% of patients confirmed after phone reminders versus 50% after text messages; studies found 6% to 12% of scans inappropriate under CAR referral guidelines; peer review of radiologist reports was not mandatory and three of four audited hospitals had a regular program; 69% of MRI machines ran below 16 hours a day, seven days a week; 65% of semi-urgent and non-urgent MRI patients and 33% of CT patients waited longer than target in 2017/18

assumptions: One report per exam; multi-part exams read together count once.
The case starts when the study is on the worklist; protocolling and ultrasound checks happen during the exam and sit in dx-imaging-exam.

The organisation file lists only the radiologist for this process; the imaging clerk and the transcriptionist are added because they handle outside priors, physician tracking, failed deliveries and the remaining transcribed dictations.
Health Report Manager (hrm) is added as a system because it is not in the organisation file; reports for clinic orders go back to amb-clinic-visit, a link the organisation file lacks.
Peer review and addenda happen after delivery but are drawn on the same path, which adds days to about 3% of simulated cases; this barely moves the median.

Simulated median cycle time is 0.9 days against a tier C benchmark of 0.8 days, and the 90th percentile 2.9 days; the median is set by outpatient studies, which are half the volume and queue behind emergency and inpatient work.

Simulated hands-on time implies about 30 FTE at 130 productive hours a month, of which about 27 are radiologist reading; 24 radiologist FTE are stated because fee-for-service radiologists work more than 130 reading hours a month, and the 30 radiologists in the organisation file (about 10,000 exams each a year) can cover the load.
Radiologist cost is the organisation file's estimate of gross clinical earnings per hour; radiologists are paid by OHIP, not the hospital.
